Question: Is it possible for a dog with no visible signs of rabies to still carry and transmit the disease to humans or other animals? If so, what are the chances of this occurring?
Answer: Possibly, but only for around 24 hours or so before symptoms begin. So the chances are quite low. (The exact chances depend on whether rabies is common in dogs in your region). There’s no such thing as an asymptomatic carrier of rabies. Any animal infected with rabies will eventually develop symptoms, and die. Rabies is only infectious (able to be passed on) about 24 hours before symptoms begin, and while the animal actually has symptoms. Dogs with rabies symptoms will die in less than 10 days. Rabies can incubate for weeks, months, or in a few rare cases, even years - but an animal incubating rabies is not infectious. It can only pass the virus once the disease becomes ACTIVE - a day before, and during, the time that it shows actual symptoms.

Question: If the kookaburra and budgerigar are only found native in Australia, does that mean they can only evolve in Australia?
Answer: No. They can (and will) evolve wherever they happen to be. Provided they don’t become extinct. Once an organism is extinct, it can’t evolve any longer. ;) They DID originally evolve in Australia, but as with all living things, they continue to evolve. Anywhere there’s a population of these birds, they will continue to evolve. Eventually, they will no longer be kookaburras or budgerigars. Kookaburras have been introduced to New Zealand, and are an invasive species there. They will continue to evolve in New Zealand unless eradicated. Budgerigars have been introduced to and are breeding in Florida in the United States. They will continue to evolve there unless eradicated. The South Florida budgies are already genetically distinct as they are escaped semi-domesticated animals from the pet trade.

Question: Did dinosaurs have a similar nesting behavior to modern birds, or did they have other methods of protecting their eggs and hatchlings?
Answer: They had similar nesting behavior to modern birds (and modern birds are, in fact, dinosaurs), and also had additional nesting behaviors seen in other reptiles. Dinosaurs were a diverse bunch. Birds have more diverse nesting behaviors than most people realize. This is a brush turkey. It lives in Australia, and it nests in a similar fashion to an alligator. It’s built that big mound of moist, rotting vegetation. Its eggs are buried in there, using the heat of the decaying vegetation to keep them warm. The bird guards the mound and adds or subtracts vegetation to control the temperature, just as alligators do with their mound nests. Some dinosaurs buried their eggs in sand or soil and left them, as turtles do. Some would create mounds like this to incubate their eggs, and guard them. Some would sit on their eggs, as most birds do. Some young dinosaurs were on their own from the moment they hatched, some were looked after by their parents, and some stayed in the nest and were fed by their parents. Modern birds use all three tactics.

Question: Why are birds closer to being a dinosaur than turtles, alligators, lizards, and snakes?
Answer: Birds are not closer to being dinosaurs. Birds are dinosaurs. This took scientists some time to realize. Dinosaurs are warm-blooded, feathered animals. It seems most likely that the first proto-feathers evolved in the Avemetatarsalians that both dinosaurs and pterosaurs evolved from, because they have now found down feathers on a pterosaur. It’s extremely unlikely that the same structures evolved twice, so their joint ancestor must have had them. And it must have been warm-blooded, because ectotherms (cold-blooded animals) don’t have insulation - it would be detrimental to them. Only endotherms and mesotherms have insulation. Some dinosaurs lost their feathers. Very large animals living in a tropical climate have more problems shedding heat than retaining it, so they didn’t need insulation. You see the same thing with rhinos and elephants in Africa. But many dinosaurs had quills, and various types of feathers. There’s not much unique about birds, with that in mind. They’re no different from other dinosaurs than bats are different from other mammals.
